lines: In this episode, we put the law into practice with the book's scenarios.
You must be able to make decisions about lethal force in scenarios like these, and your formative exam uses them.

scenes.heading: Scenario 1
bullets: Use of force in effecting an arrest
Govender vs The Minister of Safety and Security
Supreme Court of Appeal, Case No. 342/99
lines: Scenario 1 is about the use of force in effecting an arrest.
It is a real life example: Govender versus The Minister of Safety and Security.
It was heard in the Supreme Court of Appeal, case number 342 of 99.

scenes.question: Are the actions of the policemen justifiable?
lines: Two policemen chase a motor vehicle reported as stolen.
The vehicle crashes, and a number of suspects get out and run from it.
It is apparent that the suspects are youths, and they are not carrying any form of weapon.
The policemen chase one of the suspects, and issue a verbal warning that they are the police, followed by a warning shot.
The suspect does not stop, and is then shot and paralysed by one of the police officers.
Are the actions of the policemen justifiable?
reveal: No. The actions of the policemen were unreasonable and therefore unlawful.
A court did not afford the policeman the protection of Section 49, because he was clearly not acting in self defence.
The offence was not so serious as to warrant shooting the suspect.
It was an offence involving stolen property, and not violence against another human being.

scenes.heading: Bear in mind
bullets: 16.2 Everybody has the right to life
16.4 The offence: theft of a motor vehicle
lines: The book asks you to bear four things in mind.

lines.text: One. The presumption of innocence: you must be found guilty of an offence in a court of law, and not by a policeman trying to arrest you.
Two. Everybody has the right to life, including a suspect or criminal.
Three. The right to property is secondary to that of the right to life.
Four. The offence in this example is theft of a motor vehicle, which is property.

scenes.question: Have they committed an offence that justifies the use of any force against them?
lines: Scenario 2 is about self defence.
You are at home alone, in an isolated area, far from police or security services.
You look out of your window, and see two strange men jump over your wall and make their way towards your house.
You do not know these men, and you are not expecting any visitors, because it is very late at night.
Have they committed an offence that justifies the use of any force against them?
reveal: No. They are merely trespassing, which is regarded as a minor property offence.

scenes.question: Can you discharge a firearm at this point?
lines: The men come to your house, break off the burglar bars of one of your windows, and enter your house through the window.
They go to your lounge, and start to remove your extremely expensive flat screen TV.
Can you discharge a firearm at this point?
reveal: No. There is no attack against you.
Your use of force in such circumstances is not proportional to the offence being committed.
And you cannot take someone's life to protect property.

scenes.heading: Life before property
bullets: No definitive legal decision on killing to protect property
Consensus: the right to life takes precedence
Killing to protect property would be unlawful
lines: Note that there is no definitive legal decision on whether you can kill somebody to protect your property.
But the general consensus of legal experts is that the right to life takes precedence over the right to property.
And therefore, to kill somebody to protect property would be unlawful.

rule.text: You can only use force to protect your life or that of another person, and not to protect property.

lines: So the principle is this.
You can only use force to protect your life or that of another person, and not to protect property.

scenes.question: Can you discharge a firearm at them because you fear for your life?
lines: Scenario 3.
The burglars stealing your flat screen TV become aware of your presence.
They turn, and order you to go away or they will kill you.
You are behind a security gate, ten metres away.
Can you discharge a firearm at them because you fear for your life?
reveal: No. You cannot use force, because the burglars cannot directly attack you, because you are separated by a security gate.

scenes.heading: Scenario 4
scenes.caption: Both burglars are armed
lines: Scenario 4.
This time, there is no security gate between you and the burglars.
They turn around, and both are armed, one with a knife and the other with a firearm in their hands.

scenes.question: Can you discharge a firearm at them because you fear for your life?
lines: And they advance towards you.
Can you discharge a firearm at them because you fear for your life?
reveal: Yes. In such circumstances, it is reasonable to believe that they intend on killing you.
You are quite entitled to use proportional force to stop the attack, which is now imminent.
And this would include the use of lethal force.

scenes.heading: Not only a firearm
bullets: Self defence is not limited to a firearm
You can use any means at your disposal
lines: It is important to note that the right to self defence is not limited to the use of a firearm.
You can use any means at your disposal to defend yourself.
The book illustrates this with one more example.

scenes.question: Is this legally justifiable?
lines: You and your wife are stationary at a busy intersection, facing a red traffic light and waiting for it to change to green.
Your wife screams that a man is advancing towards the vehicle from the front left hand side, with a firearm in his hand.
As you look towards the would-be hijacker, he discharges two shots into your vehicle.
You drive straight towards the attacker and run him over, to prevent him from firing more shots.
In the process, you kill him.
Is this legally justifiable?
reveal: Yes. There was an unlawful attack against you.
The attack had commenced, and the means you used to stop the attack was absolutely necessary.
You directed your defence against the attacker, and there was no other way to prevent him from firing more shots.
The use of force, in the circumstances, was reasonable, and your actions therefore were legally justifiable.

points: Govender: shooting over stolen property was unlawful
Trespassing is a minor property offence
You cannot take a life to protect property
Separated by a security gate: no force
Armed and advancing: proportional, even lethal, force
Any means of defence, not only a firearm
lines: So, in the Govender case, shooting a suspect over stolen property was unreasonable and therefore unlawful.
Strangers crossing your wall are merely trespassing, a minor property offence.
You cannot take someone's life to protect property.
Behind a security gate, the burglars cannot directly attack you, so you cannot use force.
Armed burglars advancing on you may be stopped with proportional force, including lethal force.
And self defence is not limited to a firearm: you can use any means at your disposal.
